EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRETATION__Diagnost:
Sensitivity and specificity are the two core measures of a diagnostic test's intrinsic accuracy — how well it distinguishes people who truly have a disease from those who do not. They are derived from the 2×2 contingency table comparing the test result against a reference ("gold") standard, and they underpin how we choose tests for screening versus confirmation.

1THE 2×2 TABLE & DEFINITIONS

Every subject falls into one of four cells depending on their test result and their true disease status:

✅True Positive (TP)
Diseased AND test positive — correctly detected
⚠️False Positive (FP)
Healthy but test positive — false alarm
❌False Negative (FN)
Diseased but test negative — missed case
🧪True Negative (TN)
Healthy AND test negative — correctly cleared
Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) — the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. Also called the detection rate; a highly sensitive test has few false negatives.
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) — the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. A highly specific test has few false positives.
2WORKED EXAMPLE

Suppose a new blood test is evaluated in 1000 people. The gold standard finds 100 truly have the disease and 900 do not. The test gives:

Of the 100 diseased: 90 test positive (TP = 90), 10 test negative (FN = 10).
Of the 900 healthy: 810 test negative (TN = 810), 90 test positive (FP = 90).
Sensitivity = 90 / (90 + 10)→= 90% detect 9 of every 10 true cases
Specificity = 810 / (810 + 90)→= 90% correctly clear 9 of every 10 healthy people

Note both are calculated down the columns (by true disease status), which is why they do not depend on how common the disease is in the tested population.

3INTERPRETATION, THRESHOLDS & ROC

For a test with a continuous read-out (e.g. a hormone level), moving the positivity cut-off trades one property against the other. The ROC curve plots sensitivity against (1 − specificity) across all cut-offs, and the area under the curve (AUC) summarises overall discrimination.

Highly SENSITIVE test, result NEGATIVE→rules the disease OUT (SnNOut)
Highly SPECIFIC test, result POSITIVE→rules the disease IN (SpPIn)
Shift cut-off LOWER→more sensitive, less specific (catches more, more false alarms)
Shift cut-off HIGHER→more specific, less sensitive (fewer false alarms, misses more)
ROC AUC ≈ 1.0→excellent discrimination (perfect test)
ROC AUC = 0.5→no better than chance a coin toss useless test
4CLINICAL APPLICATION & PITFALLS
Screening favours sensitivity: you want to miss as few true cases as possible, accepting some false positives that a later test will sort out (e.g. HIV ELISA, antenatal screening).
Confirmation favours specificity: once screened positive, a specific confirmatory test avoids wrongly labelling healthy people (e.g. HIV Western blot / confirmatory assay).
Because sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test, they are broadly stable across populations — but spectrum bias can inflate apparent accuracy if a test is validated only in clearly diseased versus clearly healthy people rather than the borderline cases seen in practice.
No single cut-off maximises both simultaneously; the chosen threshold reflects the clinical cost of a missed case versus a false alarm.
🚩 Do NOT confuse sensitivity/specificity (properties of the TEST) with predictive values (properties of the RESULT for a patient). Positive and negative predictive values depend heavily on disease prevalence. In a low-prevalence setting even a very good test yields many false positives, so a positive result from a sensitive screening test reassures little on its own and always needs confirmation — whereas a negative from a sensitive test is genuinely reassuring.
🎓 Remember the mnemonics: SnNOut — a highly Sensitive test that is Negative rules a disease Out; SpPIn — a highly Specific test that is Positive rules a disease In. Screening favours sensitivity; confirmation favours specificity.
Combining two tests→Parallel (positive if either is positive) maximises sensitivity — good for ruling out; series (positive only if both positive) maximises specificity — good for ruling in.
Overall accuracy = (TP+TN)/N→can be deceptively high in rare disease (call everyone negative) — which is why sensitivity and specificity are reported separately. Both also assume a perfect reference standard.
EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRETATION__Predicti:
Predictive values answer the question a patient actually asks: "given my result, do I have the disease or not?" Positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a person with a POSITIVE test truly has the disease; negative predictive value (NPV) is the probability that a person with a NEGATIVE test truly is disease-free. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, which are fixed properties of the test, PPV and NPV shift with the PREVALENCE (pre-test probability) of disease in the population being tested.

1INDICATION — why predictive values matter
Sensitivity and specificity are measured in study populations where disease status is already known, so they describe how the test performs on diseased vs non-diseased people. But in the clinic you have the OPPOSITE information: you know the result, not the truth. Predictive values convert test performance into the answer the patient needs. Because they combine test accuracy with the background rate of disease, they are the practical bridge between a test result and a clinical decision.
🧪TP
true positive: test +, disease present
🧪FP
false positive: test +, no disease
🧪TN
true negative: test −, no disease
🧪FN
false negative: test −, disease present
2HOW IT IS CALCULATED — the formulae
Draw a 2×2 table (disease down the columns, test result across the rows) and read along the rows. PPV uses the top row (all positives), NPV uses the bottom row (all negatives).
PPV = TP / (TP + FP) — of everyone who tested positive, the fraction who truly have disease.
NPV = TN / (TN + FN) — of everyone who tested negative, the fraction who truly are disease-free.
Contrast: sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) and specificity = TN/(TN+FP) read down the columns, so they are independent of how common disease is.
Formally, PPV rises and NPV falls as prevalence increases; both can be recomputed from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence using Bayes’ theorem.
3INTERPRETATION — the prevalence effect with a worked example
Take ONE test with fixed sensitivity 99% and specificity 95%, and apply it in two settings.
High-prevalence clinic (pre-test 50%, 1000 patients): 500 diseased → 495 TP, 5 FN. 500 well → 475 TN, 25 FP. PPV = 495/(495+25) = 95%. A positive result almost certainly means disease.
Low-prevalence screening (pre-test 0.1%, 100000 people): 100 diseased → 99 TP, 1 FN. 99900 well → ~94905 TN, ~4995 FP. PPV = 99/(99+4995) ≈ 1.9%. The SAME test now gives ~50 false alarms for every true case.
LOW prevalence (public screening)→PPV falls sharply; most positives are FALSE positives
HIGH prevalence / symptomatic clinic patient→PPV rises; a positive is much more likely to be real
Very LOW prevalence + negative test→NPV very high; a negative is strongly reassuring
Rising prevalence across settings→PPV goes UP, NPV goes DOWN (same test)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Predictive values quoted in a package insert or textbook are only valid for the prevalence of the population in which they were derived — never transplant them to a different setting. This is why a screening programme must be targeted at a group with high enough prevalence to keep PPV useful, and why an incidental positive in a low-risk person should trigger caution rather than alarm. Always anchor a result to the individual patient’s pre-test probability (age, symptoms, risk factors) before acting.
🚩 A positive result from screening a LOW-prevalence population is often a FALSE positive. This is the mathematical basis for why indiscriminate mass screening causes harm — false alarms, over-investigation, invasive follow-up and patient anxiety — even with a highly specific test. Always interpret a result against the patient’s pre-test probability, not the test’s headline accuracy.
🎓 Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do NOT. In a low-prevalence population even a very specific test produces many false positives, so PPV is low — whereas NPV is high, making a negative result the more informative one.
Positive screening test in a low-prevalence population→low PPV — treat as provisional: confirm with a definitive diagnostic test before diagnosing/treating; counsel that a positive is not a diagnosis and most such positives are false.
Negative test in a low-prevalence population→very high NPV — reliably excludes disease, supporting reassurance/discharge without further testing.
EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRETATION__Likeliho:
A likelihood ratio (LR) combines sensitivity and specificity into a single number that tells you how much a given test result shifts the odds that a patient has the disease. Its power is that it is independent of prevalence: unlike positive/negative predictive values, an LR is a fixed property of the test itself and can be applied to any patient once you have estimated their pre-test probability.

1INDICATION — why LRs beat predictive values

Sensitivity and specificity describe a test in the abstract; predictive values answer the clinical question (“given this result, does my patient have the disease?”) but they swing wildly with prevalence. Likelihood ratios solve this by expressing test performance as a multiplier on the odds of disease, letting you formally update a pre-test estimate into a post-test estimate using Bayes' theorem.

LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) — how much a POSITIVE result raises the odds of disease.
LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity — how much a NEGATIVE result lowers the odds of disease.
2HOW IT IS APPLIED — odds and the Fagan nomogram

LRs act on odds, not probability, so you must convert first. The chain is: pre-test odds × LR = post-test odds, then convert back to probability.

probability → odds→odds = p / (1 − p); e.g. p = 0.20 gives odds 0.20/0.80 = 0.25
odds → probability→p = odds / (1 + odds); e.g. odds 0.25 gives 0.25/1.25 = 0.20

The Fagan nomogram does this graphically: draw a straight line from your pre-test probability (left axis) through the LR (centre axis) and read the post-test probability off the right axis — no arithmetic required. Because LRs are just multipliers, results from sequential tests can be chained.

3INTERPRETATION — cut-offs and SpPIn / SnNOut
LR+ > 10→strong evidence to rule IN disease (large increase in post-test probability)
LR− < 0.1→strong evidence to rule OUT disease (large decrease in post-test probability)
LR ~ 1→result changes nothing — a clinically useless test
Specific test + Positive result (high LR+)→rules IN — SpPIn
Sensitive test + Negative result (low LR−)→rules OUT — SnNOut
🧪LR+ > 10
convincing rule-in result
📈LR+ 5–10
moderate rise in probability
📉LR− 0.1–0.2
moderate fall in probability
⚖️LR ~ 1
uninformative test
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
LRs quantify the strength of a result but never give a probability on their own — you must supply a sensible pre-test probability.
A dichotomous LR discards information; stratum-specific (multilevel) LRs for graded results (e.g. a troponin band) are more informative than a single positive/negative cut-off.
Published LRs are only as good as the study spectrum they came from; spectrum bias can inflate them if the study compared florid cases with healthy controls.
🚩 A test result must ALWAYS be combined with the pre-test probability. Even a very high LR+ can leave the post-test probability low if the pre-test probability was tiny — e.g. pre-test 1% (odds ~0.01) × LR+ 15 gives post-test odds ~0.15, i.e. only ~13% probability. Never act on a positive result in isolation.
🎓 Remember the anchors: LR+ > 10 rules in, LR− < 0.1 rules out, and LR = 1 is a worthless test. LRs are prevalence-independent, work via pre-test odds × LR = post-test odds, and can be read straight off the Fagan nomogram. SpPIn (Specific + Positive = rule In); SnNOut (Sensitive + Negative = rule Out).
Full interpretation ladder→LR+ >10 large / 5–10 moderate / 2–5 small; LR− <0.1 large / 0.1–0.2 moderate / 0.2–0.5 small; LR ~0.5–2 = negligible shift; LR = 1 useless.
Nomogram-free shortcut (McGee)→LRs of 2 / 5 / 10 raise probability by roughly +15 / +30 / +45 percentage points; 0.5 / 0.2 / 0.1 lower it by ~15 / 30 / 45 points (mid-range).
Multi-level (stratum-specific) LRs→each result band carries its own LR — a strongly positive result shifts probability far more than a weakly positive one; dichotomising a graded test (troponin, D-dimer, calcium score) discards this information. Chaining sequential LRs assumes the tests are independent given disease status.
EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRETATION__Screenin:
Screening is the systematic testing of an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population to identify individuals at higher risk of a disease (or its precursor) so that earlier intervention improves outcomes. It is not diagnosis: a positive screen selects people for further diagnostic work-up, not treatment. Because screening actively invites well people to be tested, the bar for benefit is high — the WHO Wilson & Jungner criteria (1968) remain the classic framework, conventionally grouped around the condition, the test, the treatment and the programme.

1PURPOSE — why screen an asymptomatic population

Many diseases have a detectable latent or pre-clinical phase during which the process is present but not yet symptomatic. Intervening in this window can halt progression (e.g. removing a pre-malignant cervical lesion) or start treatment before irreversible damage. Screening therefore aims to shift the point of detection earlier in the natural history and reduce disease-specific mortality or morbidity.

Screening ≠ diagnosis — it stratifies risk; abnormal results need a definitive diagnostic test.
Target is the whole eligible population, most of whom are healthy, so even small harms are multiplied across millions.
Success is measured by improved outcome (e.g. mortality reduction), not merely by finding more disease.
2THE WILSON & JUNGNER CRITERIA

The classic ten criteria map onto four domains. Each cp-clue below shows the domain and what it demands.

CONDITION→An important health problem with a recognisable latent / early symptomatic stage and an adequately understood natural history
TEST→Simple, safe, acceptable to the population and valid (suitable sensitivity/specificity) with an agreed cut-off
TREATMENT→An accepted, effective treatment exists, and treating the early/latent stage improves outcome more than treating late
PROGRAMME→Cost-effective, a continuous (not one-off) process, with agreed policy on whom to treat and adequate facilities for diagnosis and treatment
🩺Cervical
hrHPV primary test, women 25–64
🎗️Breast
mammography, women 50–71, 3-yearly
💩Bowel
FIT, ages 50–74, 2-yearly
🫀AAA
one-off USS, men aged 65
🤰Antenatal
infections, Down's, anomaly scan
🍼Newborn bloodspot
day 5 heel-prick: CF, CHT, SCD, 9 conditions
3INTERPRETING SCREENING PERFORMANCE

The cut-off chosen trades sensitivity against specificity. In population screening a false negative gives false reassurance, while a false positive triggers anxiety and invasive follow-up in a well person. Positive predictive value is heavily driven by low disease prevalence.

Lower the cut-off→↑ sensitivity, ↓ specificity — catches more true cases but more false positives
Low prevalence→Low PPV even with a good test — most positives are false alarms
Positive screen→Refer for a definitive diagnostic test — do not treat on the screen alone
4BIASES & PITFALLS THAT FAKE BENEFIT

Screen-detected patients can appear to survive longer without living any longer — two biases explain why survival-time comparisons are misleading.

Lead-time bias — earlier detection advances the diagnosis date, so measured survival from diagnosis lengthens even if the date of death is unchanged.
Length-time bias — screening preferentially catches slow-growing, indolent tumours (longer pre-clinical phase), which have a better prognosis anyway; aggressive fast cancers surface between screens.
Overdiagnosis — detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime, leading to overtreatment and its harms.
Selection / healthy-volunteer bias — those who attend tend to be healthier, exaggerating apparent benefit.

This is why programme benefit is judged on disease-specific mortality in randomised trials, not on 5-year survival from screen detection.

🚩 Screening is NOT automatically beneficial. In a large healthy population it can cause net harm through false positives (anxiety, invasive follow-up), overdiagnosis and overtreatment of disease that would never have harmed the person, and radiation or procedural risk. Apparent survival gains may be illusory because of lead-time and length-time bias. A programme should run only if it meets the Wilson & Jungner criteria and evidence shows it does more good than harm.
🎓 Remember Wilson & Jungner as four boxes: an important CONDITION with a latent stage and known natural history + a valid, safe, acceptable TEST with an agreed cut-off + an effective early TREATMENT that beats late treatment + a cost-effective, continuous PROGRAMME with the facilities to follow up. And always flag lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis as reasons screen-detected survival looks falsely good.
Who decides which programmes run?→the UK National Screening Committee (NSC) appraises the evidence against modernised Wilson–Jungner criteria (RCT benefit, cost-effectiveness, acceptable harm–benefit) and advises the four UK governments to introduce, modify or stop a programme.
Screening invites well people who may be harmed→so it requires informed choice — participants must understand the benefits and harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, overtreatment) and may decline.
How a programme is structured→a high-sensitivity screen (minimise missed cases) → a confirmatory diagnostic test on positives regains specificity.
UK newborn screening = three programmes→bloodspot (day 5, 9 conditions), newborn hearing (OAE ± AABR), and NIPE (physical exam at 72 h & 6–8 weeks: eyes, heart, hips, testes).
Cervical screening intervals→hrHPV primary: 25–49 every 3 years, 50–64 every 5 years; HPV-positive samples reflexed to cytology.
Will Rogers phenomenon (stage migration)→better detection reclassifies borderline cases into “worse” stages — apparently improving stage-specific survival in every group with no real change.
EVIDENCE & TEST INTERPRETATION__Notifiab:
Notification of infectious disease is a statutory public-health duty: under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, a registered medical practitioner in England who has reasonable clinical suspicion that a patient has a notifiable disease (or a related infection posing significant harm) must report this to the proper officer of the local authority / UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The whole point is speed: notification is triggered on clinical suspicion, not on laboratory confirmation, so that contact tracing and outbreak control can begin before delay allows further spread.

1INDICATION — why the system exists

Surveillance of communicable disease lets public-health teams detect outbreaks early, identify sources, protect contacts, and monitor the impact of control measures and vaccination programmes. The duty is legal, not discretionary: it applies whenever a doctor suspects a listed disease on clinical grounds.

Who must notify: the attending registered medical practitioner (clinical suspicion).
Also mandated: diagnostic laboratories must separately report specified notifiable causative organisms once identified.
To whom: the proper officer of the local authority, working with UKHSA health-protection teams.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the process

The clinician completes a statutory notification form and sends it to the proper officer. Timing is graded by urgency of the threat.

Urgent case (e.g. suspected meningococcal disease, diphtheria, VHF)→Notify the proper officer the SAME day, usually by telephone
Routine notifiable disease→Written notification within 3 days (verbal within 24 h if urgent)
Confirmed notifiable organism in the lab→Laboratory reports separately to UKHSA
3INTERPRETATION — the golden rule and the list
Clinical suspicion of a notifiable disease→Notify PROMPTLY — do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation
Purpose of notifying early→Contact tracing, prophylaxis, outbreak detection and control
HIV infection→NOT statutorily notifiable in the UK (confidentiality) — monitored via voluntary surveillance

Common examples on the statutory list:

🦠Measles / Mumps / Rubella
Vaccine-preventable; notify on clinical suspicion
🧠Meningococcal disease / meningitis
Urgent — enables contact prophylaxis
🫁Tuberculosis
Contact tracing and treatment monitoring
💧Cholera / Food poisoning
Source identification, water/food safety
😷Diphtheria / Whooping cough
Vaccine-preventable; urgent contact action
🩸Viral haemorrhagic fever / Rabies
Same-day, high-consequence infections
🟡Acute infectious hepatitis
Hepatitis A/B/C/E — source and contacts
🩺HUS / Malaria / COVID-19
Also on the notifiable list
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Waiting for the lab: the commonest error — confirmation can take days, during which an outbreak spreads.
Assuming someone else will do it: the duty rests with the attending clinician; notify even if you suspect the case is already known.
Under-notification: surveillance data are only as good as clinician compliance, so the true burden may be underestimated.
HIV/STIs: managed through confidential voluntary surveillance rather than the statutory route.
🚩 Notification is a legal duty triggered by clinical SUSPICION, not laboratory confirmation. It is a statutory, not a discretionary, responsibility — failing to notify (or delaying until results return) obstructs contact tracing, prophylaxis and outbreak control, and is a breach of the regulations.
🎓 On clinical suspicion of a notifiable disease, notify the proper officer at the local authority / UKHSA promptly and without waiting for lab results (urgent cases by phone the same day). Know the common notifiable diseases (measles, meningococcal disease, TB, food poisoning, VHF, etc.) — and remember that HIV is NOT on the statutory list in the UK.
Common infections that are NOT statutorily notifiable→HIV/STIs, influenza, chickenpox (varicella), and the common cold — the classic “which is NOT notifiable?” traps.
Notification vs confidentiality→statutory notification is a lawful disclosure without patient consent (public-interest/statutory basis) — you notify even if the patient objects (contrast HIV, kept confidential and non-statutory).
Suspected meningococcal disease→notify same day by phone → UKHSA arranges single-dose ciprofloxacin (or rifampicin) prophylaxis for close/household contacts. Meningococcal disease ›
What happens after notification (exclusion)→e.g. measles: off school until 4 days after rash onset; a symptomatic food handler (D&V): excluded from work until 48 h symptom-free.
TB notified→contacts screened with IGRA/Mantoux; smear-positive pulmonary TB is the priority for tracing. Tuberculosis ›
More notifiable examples→scarlet fever, invasive group A strep, enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever, tetanus (alongside measles/mumps/rubella, pertussis, TB, meningococcal disease, food poisoning, acute hepatitis, HUS).
